question: How is the opening wa-annahu read and connected to the surrounding speech?

positions.position: With fatḥa, the clause is governed by revelation and belongs to God's report.
positions.reasons: Ibn Qutayba makes it accusative and coordinated with previous clauses; Sībawayh, al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Rāzī, al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr relate it to 72:1, with some allowing an independent start. Ibn ʿĀshūr parses the pronoun as one of affair. Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr and most readers read fatḥa; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the jinn quotation had ended by 72:18. Al-Ṭabrisī also records Sībawayh's independent start after quoted speech and a conditional fāʾ, with examples at 5:115 and 72:23.

positions.position: With kasra, it opens an independent divine assertion or quoted command to say the assertion.
positions.reasons: Nāfiʿ and Abū Bakr from ʿĀṣim read kasra, with other transmitters Ibn Hurmuz and Ṭalḥa. Al-Ālūsī allows a fresh divine account; Elmalılı prefers it because an intervening verse makes continuity with jinn speech awkward. Ibn ʿĀshūr coordinates with 'it was revealed to me' and supplies 'say'; he rejects continuing jinn speech after 72:18.

positions.position: With kasra, the words continue the jinn's report to their people.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr relate the jinn's description of the Companions. Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects Noah here as strained. Al-Wāḥidī argues third-person self-reference is awkward for the Prophet; al-Rāzī calls it possible and compares 19:85. Al-Kashf favors continuity if the mosques prohibition addressed the jinn; Ibn ʿĀshūr and Elmalılı object that the report was interrupted.

turns_on: Whether the hamza is governed by the revelation verb or begins a sentence, and whether the jinn's quotation has ended.

question: Who is called God's servant?

positions.position: Muhammad, the Prophet.
positions.reasons: This is explicit or called unanimous by al-Wāḥidī and al-Rāzī; 72:20 confirms it for Ṭabāṭabāʾī. Ibn ʿĀshūr relates the title to 17:1. The setting is usually his prayer or proclamation.

positions.position: Noah, whose disbelieving people pressed upon him and nearly killed him.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls this strained in the sequence. Abū Ḥayyān calls it remote; al-Ālūsī rejects it as remote.

positions.position: ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām.
positions.reasons: Abū Ḥayyān calls this even farther fetched than Noah; al-Ālūsī finds it less credible.

positions.position: In an inward reading, the servant is the heart turned toward truth.
positions.reasons: Al-Qāshānī describes the heart as humble, obedient, seeking divine light, and glorifying God.

turns_on: Whether the title is read in the Prophet's historical scene, a remote report about Noah or Ibn Salām, or the inward scene.

question: What is conveyed by calling him 'God's servant'?

positions.position: It expresses the Prophet's humility and honored, complete servitude to God.
positions.reasons: Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī and al-Rāzī discuss humble self-reference. Bursevī says ʿAbd Allāh is a beloved name, tied to the Night Journey (17:1), the Criterion (25:1), and unmatched servitude; a Persian couplet contrasts it with kings. Ālūsī, Ibn ʿĀshūr, Iṣlāḥī, Kuranyolu and Study Quran see honor or the highest spiritual station in this title; al-Sāmarrāʾī defines chosen servitude as devotion to God's pleasure.

positions.position: The title shows that a servant worshipping his own Lord is natural and gives no cause for hostile amazement.
positions.reasons: Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Rāzī contrast rational worship with the opposition it drew. Al-Biqāʿī says worship of another would be the astonishing act, and even an ordinary master's servant should not be treated this way. Iṣlāḥī notes opposition even in the house built for God's worship.

positions.position: The title identifies servanthood as the reason he stood to worship.
positions.reasons: Al-Bayḍāwī and Bursevī make the title the cause of his standing; al-Ālūsī says it suits an obedient transmission of revelation. Ṭabāṭabāʾī sees preparation for 'I invoke my Lord' in the next verse.

positions.position: The Prophet conveys God's own third-person wording without inserting himself.
positions.reasons: Al-Ālūsī says this removes any trace of personal intervention from the transmitted account.

turns_on: The notes variously stress humility, honor, the reason for worship, the obviousness of serving God, or exact transmission.

question: What does qāma mean here?

positions.position: He stood or rose for prayer and worship.
positions.reasons: Ibn al-Jawzī gives the bodily upright posture as the root sense. Reports set the action at prayer, often the dawn prayer at Nakhlah. Al-Qāshānī gives the inward equivalent as the heart's turning toward truth.

positions.position: He undertook the public call or mission to God's oneness.
positions.reasons: Ibn al-Jawzī notes qāma for undertaking a call and also for an event's arising, like the Hour. Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 18:14, al-Nābighah's line about the sons of Asad, and Juzʾ ibn Kulayb's verse about the Prophet's public worship. Al-Ḥasan places Arab opposition when he proclaimed monotheism.

turns_on: Whether the standing denotes the observed prayer or rising to undertake public proclamation.

question: What does yadʿūhu mean, and whom was he addressing?

positions.position: He invoked and worshipped God, including through prayer and recitation.
positions.reasons: Al-Wāḥidī, al-Qurṭubī and al-Bayḍāwī explicitly gloss the verb as worship; al-Samīn describes invocation in monotheism. Al-Ālūsī and Bursevī make it circumstantial to his standing, at the dawn prayer in Nakhlah. Ibn ʿĀshūr takes 'I only call upon my Lord' in 72:20 as its explanation.

positions.position: He called people to God and proclaimed His oneness.
positions.reasons: Ibn Qutayba says he called people to God; al-Ṭabarī and al-Ḥasan specify 'there is no god but God.' Ibn ʿAbbās glosses it as calling people to Him; Ibn ʿĀshūr describes public monotheistic proclamation.

positions.position: He called the jinn to God.
positions.reasons: Ibn Jurayj is reported by al-Qurṭubī; the verse's jinn scene gives the proposed addressees.

positions.position: He called the Jews to God.
positions.reasons: Al-Māwardī transmits this from Ibn Jurayj.

turns_on: Whether yadʿūhu describes worship directed to God or preaching directed to an audience; the reported audience also varies.

positions.position: It is a circumstantial clause describing the servant as he stood, invoking God.
positions.reasons: Al-Samīn, Bursevī and al-Ālūsī give this parse; Bursevī links the action to Fajr prayer at Nakhlah.

question: Who are 'they,' and why did they nearly gather over him?

positions.position: The listening jinn crowded around Muhammad in eagerness, wonder, and love for the Qur'an and his worship.
positions.reasons: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Zubayr and others give this account. Some say they nearly climbed over him or one another, approached unseen until Gabriel disclosed them (72:1), or marveled at unfamiliar prayer and recitation. Al-Ālūsī says the image implies a larger audience than nine; Bursevī replies that seven or nine at Nakhlah make a crowd unlikely, though approach from one direction could explain it.

positions.position: The Prophet's Companions crowded near him, following his prayer and showing remarkable obedience.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr say they matched his bowing and prostration, and jinn told their people of it. Al-Ṭabrisī adds that each wanted to hear and be closest. Al-Biqāʿī compares an envoy's account of orderly Muslim rows impressing a Persian king. Bursevī says few companions, perhaps only Zayd, were with him and objects to a literal crowd.

positions.position: Arab or Quraysh polytheists crowded around Muhammad in hostility to his monotheistic call.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī prefers this from the link with 72:18: opposition follows the ban on invoking another. Al-Ḥasan describes united Arabs, and Ibn ʿĀshūr derives the referent from 72:16–18; they gathered angrily to hear and intended harm. Ṭabāṭabāʾī prefers mockery and loud interruption. Asad broadens it to a recurring majority's hostility to unpopular moral truth.

positions.position: Humans and jinn jointly massed against Muhammad to extinguish his mission, but God supported it.
positions.reasons: Qatāda is the recurring authority, often with al-Ḥasan and Ibn Zayd; al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr prefer this hostile reading. Elmalılı says it fits either hamza reading and 72:13. Kuranyolu cites Ṭabarī's preference; Asad relates it to 9:32.

positions.position: Noah's disbelieving people nearly attacked him.
positions.reasons: This depends on identifying the servant as Noah; Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī call that identification strained or remote.

positions.position: In an inward reading, the faculties crowd the heart and veil it by their dominance.
positions.reasons: Al-Qāshānī interprets the servant as the heart.

positions.position: Truth-deniers repeatedly mass against any individual or minority defending an unpopular moral truth.
positions.reasons: Asad acknowledges Muhammad and his contemporaries as an initial setting, then generalizes the pattern.

turns_on: The pronoun's antecedent and the motive for gathering: listening, following in prayer, or hostile opposition.

question: What setting and further events are reported for this scene?

positions.position: At Nakhlah, jinn heard Muhammad praying and reciting, then gathered to listen.
positions.reasons: Al-Muqātil places him between Mecca and Ṭāʾif with nine jinn; al-Zubayr specifies evening prayer, while al-Zajjāj, al-Zamakhsharī and others specify dawn. Al-Biqāʿī says jinn sent toward Tihāmah by Iblīs heard his monotheism and believed. Ibn Kathīr says he did not see their approach until Gabriel informed him.

positions.position: He prayed and recited in a valley of Mecca.
positions.reasons: Al-Wāḥidī gives this location without specifying Nakhlah.

positions.position: At al-Ḥajūn, an Ibn Masʿūd account describes black men like the Zutt crowding around the Prophet after he drew Ibn Masʿūd a line.
positions.reasons: Al-Durr transmits the account as before the Hijra; Bursevī says Ibn Masʿūd's event followed Nakhlah and objects that it was witnessed rather than revealed and too few Companions were present.

positions.position: Seventy thousand jinn pledged allegiance or followed the Prophet until daybreak.
positions.reasons: Al-Qurṭubī transmits Burd from Makḥūl without grading; al-Biqāʿī cites Makḥūl from Abū Ḥayyān.

turns_on: The transmitted locations, prayer times, and numbers differ.

question: What does libadan mean here?

positions.position: Dense, layered crowds or heaps packed tightly together.
positions.reasons: The singular is libda/lubda; comparisons include felted wool, matted hair and a lion's mane, and a locust swarm. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Wāḥidī cite ʿAbd Manāf's locust verse and explain jābiya as consuming or gathering food; Ibn ʿAṭiyya also records jāni. Al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī and al-Rāzī cite Zuhayr's lion line; Dhū al-Rumma is also cited. Ibn Qutayba uses an accumulation of illicit gain. Al-Farrāʾ likens the form to plural human adjectives. Al-Naḥḥās favors the crowd sense over mere abundance and traces the root to accumulated, sticking material, including a mass of hair.

positions.position: Helpers or supporters.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿAbbās supplies this gloss in al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Naḥḥās, al-Māwardī and al-Durr; Abū Ḥayyān also reports it.

positions.position: Abundance or a great quantity.
positions.reasons: Al-Naḥḥās reports Mujāhid's alternate abundance gloss but favors gathered crowds. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī points to 90:6 and says the ḍamma form suggests numerous listeners, though kasra is more familiar here. Al-Mubarrad calls a similar form 'many' or a singular descriptive form. Al-Qurṭubī also cites abundant wealth.

positions.position: Enduring, like Luqmān's last vulture Lubad.
positions.reasons: Al-Qurṭubī cites al-Nābighah's poetry and the lore of Luqmān choosing seven vultures instead of ewes for long life; al-Samīn mentions the name.

positions.position: In another usage, al-labad is a stay-at-home person.
positions.reasons: Al-Qurṭubī reports Abū ʿUbayd's preferred transmitted variant in a line praising good judgment and large undertakings.

positions.position: A cited lion poem may refer to its thick mane, though the excerpt does not identify its lexical target.
positions.reasons: Al-Naḥḥās gives an unattributed poem of a well-armed lion with mane and unclipped claws.

turns_on: The notes offer a physical crowd image, helpers, abundance, endurance, and other related lexical usages.

question: How is libadan read and formed?

positions.position: The common reading has kasra on lām and fatḥa on bāʾ, generally a plural of libda.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī prefers the city readers' form; Abū ʿUbayda and Abū Ḥātim also prefer it in al-Thaʿlabī. Nāfiʿ, the majority, and most transmissions use it. Al-Farrāʾ and later grammarians say its sense matches the ḍamma reading. Ibn ʿĀshūr instead calls it a collective noun.

positions.position: With ḍamma on lām and a light, open bāʾ, it is a dialectal plural of lubda.
positions.reasons: Attributed variously to Ibn Muḥayṣin, Mujāhid, Hishām from Ibn ʿĀmir, and in some accounts Ibn ʿĀmir. Al-Farrāʾ and al-Ṭabarī say it has the same sense as kasra. Ibn Muḥayṣin also has a still bāʾ form. Qiraat-ER says it can emphasize distinct clusters.

positions.position: With ḍamma on both lām and bāʾ, it is related to lubd, lubūd, or lubayd.
positions.reasons: Reports attribute this to Abū Ḥaywah, al-Ḥasan, al-Jaḥdarī and others; al-Qushayrī describes lubayd as a small sack. Some parse it as a plural comparable to ṣabūr/ṣubar.

positions.position: With a doubled bāʾ, it is a plural of lābid describing the clustered people.
positions.reasons: Al-Farrāʾ compares bowing and prostrating adjective plurals; al-Zajjāj compares rākiʿ/rukkaʿ and ghāzin/ghuzā. Attributions vary among al-Ḥasan, Abū Jaʿfar, al-Jaḥdarī, Abū al-ʿĀliyah and al-Aʿraj. Abū Rajāʾ has an unusual kasra-on-lām doubled variant.

positions.position: A proposed analysis treats a related labad form as a singular descriptive adjective rather than a plural.
positions.reasons: Al-Mubarrad compares ḥaṭam for a person; al-Samīn applies this to the ḍamma form and cites 90:6.

turns_on: The vowel on lām, the vowel or doubling of bāʾ, and the related singular or plural pattern.

question: How does this statement connect with the surrounding verses?

positions.position: It continues the revelation or jinn report begun at 72:1.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī connects a jinn listening account with 72:1. Ibn ʿAṭiyya coordinates the fatḥ reading with 72:1; al-Ṭabrisī and Ibn ʿĀshūr likewise connect it to revelation. Al-Biqāʿī sets both possibilities alongside each other.

positions.position: It follows 72:18's command of exclusive worship by showing hostility to God's servant who obeyed it.
positions.reasons: Al-Ṭabarī uses this link to prefer hostile Arabs; al-Ālūsī calls it an elegant transition. Ibn ʿĀshūr traces polytheists through 72:16–18; Iṣlāḥī notes tawḥīd was opposed in the house built for it.

positions.position: The following commands clarify the Prophet's call and God's protection.
positions.reasons: Ibn ʿĀshūr says 72:20 explains yadʿūhu. Ṭabāṭabāʾī reads mission, oneness, resurrection and protection from error across these verses; Elmalılı says the commands fit their flow. Al-Ālūsī links 72:21–22 to bodily prostration points. Al-Fārisī compares qāla with imperative qul in 72:20, the latter fitting commands in 21–22.

positions.position: The passage informs the Prophet of unseen outward events and inward feelings.
positions.reasons: Elmalılı gives this as a function shared by its interpretive alternatives.

positions.position: Asad connects its recurring opposition to 19:73–74.
positions.reasons: He directs readers to those verses and their notes.

turns_on: How the clause's speaker and crowd relate to 72:1, 72:18, and the commands that follow.

question: What other lessons do these sources attach to the surrounding passage?

positions.position: Uprightness may bring Paradise and expanded provision.
positions.reasons: Al-Jishumī states both possible rewards.

positions.position: The passage calls for reflection on proofs.
positions.reasons: Al-Jishumī makes this demand explicit.

positions.position: The densely gathered crowd could be praise or blame.
positions.reasons: Al-Jishumī allows both evaluations of the phrase.

turns_on: Whether the gathering is praiseworthy or hostile, with further lessons noted for the passage.

question: What do the cited passages say about literary clarity?

positions.position: The cited verse pictures distinguished men admitted by their standing, while mere approach does not secure entry.
positions.reasons: Al-Jurjānī uses the image of kings' gates.

positions.position: Obscure verbal order makes meaning needlessly indirect; effort pleases only when the discovered meaning merits it.
positions.reasons: Al-Jurjānī likens unrewarding complexity to a miser's empty promises and faults Abū Tammām's strained diction. His line about a 'second' in the sky and two men in the cave illustrates the contrivance.

turns_on: The surrounding literary discussion contrasts a clear image with obscure construction.

question: What grammatical and recitational principles appear in ancillary citations?

positions.position: A full pause can separate utterances; a lesser pause permits only breath or no interval.
positions.reasons: Al-Zarkashī gives the distinctions.

positions.position: A pronoun of affair is third-person nominative and may introduce a clause without an antecedent.
positions.reasons: Al-Zarkashī reports grammarians parsing huwa with Allāh as second subject and aḥad as predicate; he distinguishes a separation pronoun, which may have any person and case.

positions.position: A poetic example uses masculine agreement with Barada's water.
positions.reasons: Al-Zarkashī says agreement with an overt feminine noun would take feminine tāʾ.

turns_on: The citations concern distinct grammatical examples.

question: What ancillary reports address revelation and the seven revealed forms?

positions.position: The Prophet showed physical effects when revelation came.
positions.reasons: ʿĀʾishah describes his head drooping, face changing color, cold teeth, and pearl-like sweat.

positions.position: Each of seven revealed forms is sufficient and should not be abandoned or disputed.
positions.reasons: Ibn Masʿūd rejects abandoning one form out of disdain; Abū Bakrah permits any form so long as punishment and mercy are not interchanged; ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ calls disputes over forms unbelief. ʿUthmān confirms witnesses to the Prophet's declaration.

positions.position: The seven-forms report is widely transmitted and raises questions of occasion, meaning, number, and variation.
positions.reasons: Abū ʿUbayd calls it mutawātir. Ibn al-Jazarī traces nineteen Companions and al-Suyūṭī counts twenty-one; Ibn al-Jazarī lays out ten questions.

turns_on: The ancillary reports differ in topic and detail.
